doc.title: Jimmy Wormworth interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

title: Joining Nellie Lutcher at twenty and George Clisskins's drum teaching
summary: He was confident at 20 when joining Lutcher, and credits his teacher George Clisskins and the Stone and Harr books.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Well tell me what it is like to go out and start playing with — when you started playing with Nellie Lutcher, you were how old?
I was pretty self confident. Some people would describe it as jerky or conceited maybe.

But well I loved her music and it was such a pleasure to play it and I considered myself fortunate to have fallen into this position where I could play with somebody whose music I knew so well and whose music I loved, whose work I loved. And I guess I considered myself pretty fortunate but I think somewhere in the back of my mind I thought I deserved it as well. It was pretty easy to me. I had really good chops. I had excellent training, technical training, from the late George Clisskins, who was Central New York’s — in my estimation — was Central New York’s greatest drum and percussion teacher.

Yeah, but you either took it or left it. He told you what was required and either you did it or he cut you loose. Well you want to play or don’t you? This is what you have to do for next week. He’d put an “O” on the page of work you were supposed to accomplish until your next lesson which was about a week, and then he’d put a “K” if he thought you mastered whatever exercises he had given you.

And I don’t think I remember practicing at all. I can remember one of my aunts threatening me to practice, so I must have practiced some, but I know I went through his whole course in about 2-1/2 years, from 10 to about 12-1/2, and it included a few books. It started out with a book he had written, a beginner’s book that taught you four strokes, and then taught you how to put the strokes together to make up the 26 rudiments, and then he used the Haskell Harr books which were pretty well known in that time period, the 50s, late 40s early 50s, and then he put me through George Lawrence Stone’s stick control, which is a pretty renown book, most accomplished drummers know of it, even if they didn’t study it, which I think a lot of drummers did. He was based in Boston, George Lawrence Stone, and it seems to me all the drummers I know who came from Boston, Alan Dawson, Tony Williams, who else, a couple of others, were really accomplished technicians, could play fast and complicated, and I can’t help — oh Roy Haynes of course — and I can’t help but think that George Lawrence Stone’s teaching and his book in particular influenced those guys.
